20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">Dear readers,</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Earlier this week, the House of Representatives passed the ill-named “Sunshine Protection Act” by a vote of 308 to 117. The law would require most states to adopt permanent daylight saving time — that is, the clocks would stay rolled forward all year, with solar noon generally occurring around 1pm. This is a great system for the summer, which is why we already do it in the summer. The problem is that in the winter, sunrise would often be very late — as late as 8:20 a.m. in New York, 8:30 a.m. in Dallas, 8:51 a.m. in Salt Lake City, 8:57 a.m. in Seattle, 9:01 a.m. in Detroit, and so forth. Under this regime, most Americans would be waking up in the dark, commuting to work in the dark, and sending their children to school in the dark.</p><p class="button-wrapper" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a41cedee-76a8-4675-9a2a-104e8d6f0462?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">as I’ve had to remind everyone repeatedly over the years</a><span> — we did it before and people hated it: permanent DST was trialed in 1974 and repealed due to widespread dissatisfaction, mere months into what was supposed to be a two-year “experiment.” In the House, the vote for ending the experiment and returning to seasonal DST was 383 to 16. Now, we might run that experiment again, though it’s not clear the bill will be taken up in the Senate, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eb1d15f0-7488-420b-9c53-3fd30ef358d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">where there is a fair amount of regional opposition from states where the sun would rise especially late</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This push to repeat an old mistake reflects three of the main political dysfunctions of our time:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Failure to consider trade-offs. </strong><span>We all like when the sun shines. Marco Rubio, who was the leading advocate for permanent DST when he served in the Senate, loves to wax in speeches about the wonderful uses of sunshine in the afternoon. But the government cannot create or destroy sunshine — it can only allocate it to the morning or the afternoon. Rubio’s plan to </span><strong>“</strong><span>protect</span><strong>”</strong><span> afternoon sunshine entails forcing Americans to rise and commute in the dark, which they are not going to enjoy. How do I know that? Because, unlike most people, I bother to learn what has happened in the past.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Ignorance of history.</strong><span> Advocates of permanent daylight saving time are often unaware that we tried this before — and that Congress swiftly reversed course because Americans were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9bf4c776-1563-45cb-bcad-2dcad8942587?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">very unhappy about the loss of sunlight in the morning hours</a><span>. Even when they learn this, it is rare that they update their stance. Many blindly dismiss the lessons of history; they say 1974 was a long time ago and things are different now. But the main </span><em>relevant</em><span> difference between 1974 and now is that technology handles clock changes on our behalf, so time changes are less burdensome than they used to be. I barely notice them, in fact. But I </span><em>will</em><span> notice if it’s dark out in New York City</span><strong> </strong><span>at 8 a.m. in December, and we know from history that voters will notice too and they won’t be pleased about it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;margin-bottom: 0;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 Ed Markey calls it “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf023cba-1947-428a-b7f4-d3de194924f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">a head-spinning ritual</a><span>” — if his head spins when the clock changes, maybe that’s a sign he’s too old to do the job of a U.S. Senator — while Sen. Ron Wyden calls it “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed73e0c5-9177-4ae9-87f9-5b1a3070666c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">madness</a><span>.” In a 2023 editorial advocating permanent daylight saving, the </span><em>Los Angeles Times</em><span> Editorial Board </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4a12e9c5-6504-4bee-baa3-039968dde1ea?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">wrote</a><span>, “we set the clocks forward an hour to begin daylight saving time (or increasingly, our smart devices do it automatically) and then spend the next few days slightly discombobulated and wondering why we still practice this odd ritual. By the time the following Sunday rolls around, our disturbed schedules have adjusted and we forget about the week of missed appointments or bad sleep.” Really? The grown, college-educated adults published in the LA Times miss </span><em>a week of appointments</em><span> after a time shift that occurs on a weekend and is accounted for automatically by their electronic devices? Have these people never gone on a business trip to a different time zone? How do they cope if they stay up late to watch a sporting event,</span><strong> </strong><span>or have to get up early to catch a flight? When I wrote in defense of seasonal time back in 2021, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fffb5535-3d5f-45ff-b7df-c49dc420f833?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">one reader complained to me</a><span> that clock changes are “life-ruining” for parents. Sen. James Lankford echoes this sentiment, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf023cba-1947-428a-b7f4-d3de194924f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">saying</a><span> “moms of young children dread the time of year when clocks change.” I don’t have children, but I asked my mother, who raised four children, and she says time changes were not much of a problem — and back in her day, she had to physically change the clocks when the clock changed. There is an epidemic of people in America — voters, alas — who purport to find themselves devastated and aggrieved by the slightest annoyances, especially the ones that have actually gotten less annoying over the decades. At least some of this is fake — some people just like to complain, and are not suffering to the extent they claim to be. But some of it is real, and I believe the increasing unreasonableness of an electorate that wants all its groceries in one bag and also doesn’t want the bag to be heavy</span><strong> </strong><span>is a primary driver behind permanently low approval of politicians in both parties.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I am hopeful that the Senate — as it so often does — will bottle up this piece of House-passed legislation and not allow it to</span><strong> </strong><span>become law. But if that doesn’t happen, the new “permanent” daylight saving time law will reflect a fourth political dysfunction of our time: politicians acting based on what they think polls well, rather than based on what will actually produce results that make voters happy. If a bipartisan cadre of Washington insiders chooses to plunge voters into winter darkness, that will only further erode public confidence in our political elites, and I’m confident the law will be swiftly repealed much like it was in 1974.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Very seriously,</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: For starters, everything in life is relative. The main point here is that even in a blue state that Kamala Harris won comfortably, the Democratic Party as a whole is seen as too left-wing. At the same time, the party is beset by a leftist insurgency. If people develop the view that elected leftist insurgents will stop Democrats from being viewed as too left-wing, disastrous things could happen. The correct analysis here, I think, is that Platner was well to the left of public opinion on lots of issues — notably trans issues — but so are basically all Democrats. But Platner really did articulate a forceful opposition to assault weapons bans that would put him on the rightward edge of the party. He didn’t do land acknowledgments. He didn’t talk about “birthing people” or BIPOC or Latinx. I don’t think there’s really any evidence that being a white man with tattoos was helping him massively, but these low-effort linguistic cues probably do matter. He did not </span><em><span>speak</span></em><span> like a person who was constantly worried about aligning himself with the views of left-wing campus activists, and on at least one noteworthy cultural issue — guns — he staked out a moderate position. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So I think the moral of the story here is that if you want to be perceived as more moderate, you should adopt some moderate issue positions and talk like a moderate.  </span></p><div class="subscription-widget-wrap" style="font-size: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Mike:</a><span> </span><span>I’ve seen a lot of articles framing data center opposition as evidence of strong anti-AI sentiment, but to my eyes, it looks about the same as every other bit of NIMBYism — you regularly see community opposition to solar panels, to utility-scale batteries, to apartment buildings. Do you think there’s really a uniquely anti-AI element to this, or is that just how it’s being read by journalists who are unfamiliar with the broader NIMBY context and also hate AI?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a little of both. I don’t think anyone who is familiar with the broad NIMBY context of American life is all that shocked to discover that it is frequently possible to mobilize local opposition to large-scale construction projects. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But part of the deal with NIMBYism is that people generally don’t have some kind of big concerns about apartment buildings going up on the other side of the state. That is not in your backyard. My initial read on the whole data center situation was that developers would indeed find that lots of places don’t want these projects, but also that it wouldn’t be a very big deal. There are lots of places in America, and the data centers will just go where people on net decide the tax revenue is worth the hassle. What we’re seeing in terms of political momentum for statewide bans on data centers suggests something broader than a strict backyard-based concern. Most states are pretty big. Why should you care if data centers are going up a four-hour drive from your house?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some of that reflects concerns about electricity prices, which can have less localized impacts. Still, the obvious solution to concerns about electricity prices is just to tighten up the terms on which the permits are issued. Looked at just economically, the obvious rule should be “you can build the data center only if you agree to terms that make it net beneficial to ratepayers.” That may mean a lot of proposed projects don’t get built, or it may mean they get built on terms that are beneficial to ratepayers. A </span><em><span>ban</span></em><span> doesn’t make sense. So I think you need to bring in the context that people are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa0d160f-4f3f-43ab-a9a2-94a3587132e1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>moderately skeptical of A.I.’s impact on their lives</span></a><span> and more skeptical of its impact on society. </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Rose Research</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, in response to this polling, A.I. companies have mostly pivoted away from the utopian rhetoric they used to use about this in favor of being more cuddly and reassuring. They now want you to believe that their models will be incredibly useful and productivity-enhancing but in ways that don’t disrupt the labor market, and I’m not sure how coherent that even is. Obviously, there has been a lot of technological innovation over the past 200 years that has not eliminated human labor. But it definitely </span><em><span>has</span></em><span> eliminated specific jobs or even whole fields or transformed them into barely recognizable versions of themselves or shrunk them. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So my broad take is that different kinds of worries are mutually reinforcing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is hard to build anything in the modern world. A lot of contemporary Westerners have a basically incoherent view by which they are nostalgic for a past era of more rapid change in the physical landscape, and this makes them want to make it illegal to alter the physical landscape, which leads to stagnation outcomes they don’t like, which makes them more nostalgic. But you </span><em><span>can</span></em><span> find ways to overcome this kind of knee-jerk skepticism about building new stuff. Doing that, though, requires some kind of baseline view that it would be good to have the stuff. With A.I., clearly people have a reasonably strong revealed preference for using it. But their stated views of the technology are pretty skeptical, and they are not especially worried about its progress slowing down as a result of physical construction impediments. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The big problem, it seems to me, is that altering the physical location of data centers is actually a very weak lever for making A.I. policy. Even if no data center is ever constructed in Portugal, or wherever, the lives of Portuguese people could be very disrupted by A.I. progress. As such, you need rules addressing both the economic consequences of A.I. and A.I. governance, and neither area can be addressed just with rules about data centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e8503300-c4e2-45fd-939c-38f638353ae4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Andy:</a><span> </span><span>You’ve had at least two staff members from the great state of Colorado, and there are several regulars in the comment section (including me) from Colorado. This isn’t scientific, but it seems to me we are over-represented at SB — why do you think that is?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t know if this is a coincidence or not, but the high representation of Coloradans on the team is something I’ve noticed. I would also say that in Jared Polis, John Hickenlooper, Michael Bennet, Joe Neguse, Jason Crow, and Brittany Pettersen the state has a lot of elected officials who are broadly aligned with Slow Boring policy. I think this in part reflects the fact that Blue Colorado is a very recent historical phenomenon. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back in 2004, Colorado was redder than Nevada, Ohio, or Iowa, which is just to say that the current crop of prominent elected officials is mostly people who got elected winning tough races, who take politics seriously, and who’ve advanced progressive priorities in a judicious and considered way. It’s possible that the state is now </span><em><span>so</span></em><span> blue that this won’t be the case in the future and it’ll become a quagmire like New York, where tedious machine politicians duke it out with far-left ideologues. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, I like </span><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/the-midterm-candidates-who-deserve?r=awv5d&selection=b73a9e71-2da0-4de2-85f2-0e2ca25d0d21&utm_campaign=post-share-selection&utm_medium=web&aspectRatio=instagram&textColor=%23ffffff&bgImage=true" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Manny Rutinel</span></a><span>. He just won a House primary and will hopefully beat his Republican opponent by a lot. So hope springs eternal. Maybe it’s the altitude?    </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All that being said, while I’ve been to Colorado four times in my life, they were all short trips — three for conferences and one for a wedding. I’ve never spent much time in the state and don’t really know very much about it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-051?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=293157950" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Oliver:</span></a><span> “Mamdani is telling his base what they want to hear, exploiting grievances, and then doing things they would not approve of. It’s very Trumpian.”</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Do you think </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/321a4748-452a-4a90-ac0d-0e4a567cc8ba?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>this tweet</span></a><span> is unfair? It did make me wonder how Trump and Mamdani both pair maximalist rhetoric while moderating in practice but also never admitting they’ve conceded an inch. Mamdani dresses up small bore wins as grand socialist achievements, sprinkles in lofty left wing quotations, and throws enough rhetorical chum to his base that nobody dwells too much on the policy. Trump does the right-wing version: quietly retreats, delays, or settles for less, then declares total victory and frames whatever happened as proof that only he could have delivered it. If moderates advertise every concession as responsible pragmatism, they absorb all the political cost from partisans while generating none of the excitement. How do self described moderates get out of this unhealthy dynamic and learn the trick? </span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What I think is “Trumpian” about Mamdani is that like Trump he has a base of supporters who treat his presence in office and his political successes as highly desirable political goals. To many, they both serve as </span><em><span>symbols</span></em><span> of triumph over their enemies. As a result, when Mamdani holds a very polite and cordial meeting with Trump in the White House, Mamdani fans interpret that as a display of their champion’s political mastery while they would see it as a craven sellout if someone they didn’t like did it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But you asked if it’s “unfair” to characterize Mamdani as somewhat Trumpian. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think that’s a category error. What’s </span><em><span>bad</span></em><span> about Trump is a specific kind of lawless authoritarianism. The existence of a personalistic following is aggravating to people who are not in the following, but it’s also a little bit banal. Barack Obama was like this. And so were Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. I think it’s a bad feature of Madisonian-style political institutions that they tend to encourage this style of politics. Still, one has to play the game. To me, it’s striking that Mamdani’s policies are incredibly similar to Bill de Blasio’s, complete with a substantial amount of continuity in personnel and overall the same strengths and weaknesses. But with de Blasio, progressives were constantly mad at him for not delivering wildly unrealistic forms of transformative change, whereas the Mamdani cult of personality has made his supporters more tolerant of banal realities. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The actual problem with both guys is that while New York City does have enough underlying economic strength to raise more tax revenue (and the pied-à-terre tax is clever), too much of that revenue is captured by the city’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5e76abae-a81d-4304-8ce8-2fd8edc51219?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>various stationary bandits</span></a><span> rather than translated into useful services. It would probably take someone with Mamdani-level charisma to take this problem on — we know that moderate low-rizz technocrat Michael Bloomberg couldn’t really do it. But you can’t tackle tough problems unless you acknowledge that they exist, and Mamdani is running into them. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b666e31e-1832-4843-9732-3c05c8aa4195?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>If he succeeds in making the city buses go faster</span></a><span>, for example, that could reduce overtime payments for bus drivers. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" important for Democrats to take in November, and what is the path to taking it?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a bunch of different ways to look at this, but I think the Georgia governor’s race is very important in an uncomplicated way. That’s why Keisha Lance Bottoms is on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/856af50f-a95f-43cb-9006-f023de0dacc5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Slow Boring’s donation recommendations list</span></a><span> even though she was not my first (or second or necessarily even third) choice for the nomination.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Georgia is important because it’s a large state and a lot of people live there. And it’s important in an uncomplicated way because despite being purple in its overall partisanship, the baseline public policy is very right-wing. With a conservative legislature, there’s no way a </span><span>Bottoms</span><span> administration is going to go off the rails and do dumb left-wing stuff. But there is a real chance of picking the low-hanging fruit of progressive governance such as Medicaid expansion, a small minimum-wage hike, reduced gerrymandering, and of course a state government that won’t try to help Trump steal the 2028 election. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-051?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=293160188" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>J. Willard Gibbs: </span></a><span>Taking at face value the need to elect more moderate Dems, how do we convince more of them to run for office? Or maybe more of a meta question: why do people run for office in the first place? I can tell you why I don’t: not comfortable with fame/being a public figure, don’t want my family harassed, too many cultural issues I’d need to take a stand on that I simply don’t care that much about. Right now it seems like there’s a lot of energy on the progressive side (while I don’t agree with many of their solutions, I certainly understand the appeal) and cynically, I could justify why those on the far right seem to be jumping in. So how to we bring that energy to “fight, but for well regulated capitalism and classic Liberalism that doesn’t degenerate into cultural nonsense”?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Andrew Hall’s 2019 book “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/749717ea-2681-4762-ac53-26731f9d577f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Who Wants to Run?: How the Devaluing of Political Office Drives Polarization</span></a><span>” is one of the most underrated books out there in my opinion. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What he says is, basically, that holding political office is not an objectively very desirable job for most broadly capable people, and that’s especially true of lower-ranking offices in state legislatures and so forth. Under the circumstances, the people who want to run are disproportionately kind of extreme ideologues relative to the general population. People were joking around about me filing to fill the Maine Senate vacancy, which is a good gag, but, in addition to being ineligible, I would sincerely not want the job. And not like in a humble “I’m not worthy of your high esteem” sense. It would be a huge pay cut. It would involve an annoying amount of travel. In practice, the main way members of Congress wield influence these days seems to be by posting takes — except, instead of nice columns, they are doing tons of short-form vertical video. Thanks, but no thanks. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anyways, this is a complicated question, but I do think the number one answer is to boost the compensation and staff allowances. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-051?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=293163305" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Niketas:</span></a><span> Does the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/366d73af-51e9-4d32-96a9-fe8e03ba7911?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Common Sense Manifesto</span></a><span> apply in some ways outside the US to liberalism in core allies? You’re relatively bullish on the UK/agree with swapping out Starmer: what needs to be done in France and Germany to further liberalism/human flourishing/democracy?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Ideally this would take place alongside a Mark Kelly-Jon Ossoff common sense restoration to be Europe’s ally in all this — but things do not seem to be going at all well in France or Germany politically, and growth not catching up to US. Thanks!</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are common trends around the world and things to learn, but whenever I end up on the global circuit, I am reminded that there are huge relevant differences in the status quo. One thing that immediately shows up is that because there is way more money in American politics, Democratic Party political operatives have dramatically more technical skill than their counterparts in Germany or Italy or whatever. So from a pure trade-show perspective, there’s kind of a “learning from the Americans” dynamic. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But if you think structurally about what Democrats are doing, you see that their best issues are basically “poor people should get health care” and “women should be allowed to have abortions.” These are not actually contested issues in European politics, which is just to say that beyond specific problems navigating the politics of immigration and whatnot, there’s a real question in my mind as to what a center-left pitch in continental Europe looks like. The far-right National Rally in France is just not proposing the policies that I would advise Democrats to focus on running against. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But there’s also a double movement in this. The policy status quo in Europe is less favorable to center-left parties, but underlying public opinion is also way more left-wing. European voters are more secular, less individualistic, and more concerned about climate change. So, broadly, some of the main problems Democrats are dealing with don’t really exist in German politics, but some of the main solutions available to Democrats aren’t really available there, either. The upshot is that I have limited advice!</span></p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: And I’ve listened to and enjoyed individual episodes of the shows, like the “Dwarkesh Podcast,” that I’ve never been on. But I’m not a regular listener to any of these, and I don’t think that’s a coincidence. These are shows that are so close to my work that I don’t find it </span><em>entertaining</em><span> per se to listen to Ezra or Tim or Josh. They are talking about subjects I am very well-informed about and dealing with debates that I participate in constantly. I check out an episode sometimes because I want to hear what they are saying, but audio is not a very efficient medium for synthesizing information. I really wanted to know what Bill McKibben said on “The Ezra Klein Show,” so I read the transcript. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By contrast, I would never read a transcript of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ff2678f-fc3b-460c-9932-d5f12f0e1d69?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Bill Simmons hosting Zach Lowe</a><span> to chat about the Jaylen Brown trade. But when I’m looking to fill time while driving or walking around, I love to listen to that kind of conversation about basketball. My very core podcast rotation is “The Big Picture” and “The Rewatchables,” which are both about movies, supplemented by The Ringer’s “House of the Dragon” recap pods when that show is on. I also love “The History of English Podcast” and the John McWhorter episodes of “Lexicon Valley.” I like the “Accidental Tech Podcast,” I like Lowe when the N.B.A. is in season, and I like “Blank Check” when they’re talking about movies I’m interested in. But the point is this is all stuff that’s pretty remote from my day job.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I hope that Slow Boring readers enjoy “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bb569554-b156-45b7-a269-b0e3c7c924d6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Politix</a><span>” and “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/06f6e541-436f-4fbc-b85d-cfd5844ddd46?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">The Argument</a><span>,” the two shows that I co-host, and I would anticipate that fans of those shows would enjoy a lot of the shows that you named. But I’m personally too close to this work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Incidentally, though, if someone </span><em>did</em><span> ask me to be a guest on a sports podcast, I would say that Celtics fans have gotten so wrapped around the axle about this Brown trade, and so caught up in the controversies about advanced analytics, that they are missing the forest for the trees. Last year, Boston won 56 games and finished second in the East with Jayson Tatum </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4312938c-03be-4ac3-9e64-83d199d0f4d7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">playing only 522 minutes</a><span> in total. He is better than Brown and will be back at full strength next year. Paul George, even in his diminished, elderly state, is a useful basketball player who shoots very well and is fine on defense. Last season, the Knicks got 1,175 minutes out of Mitchell Robinson. That should fully displace the 338 subpar minutes Nikola Vucevic played for Boston last year and cut into the 1,118 minutes of Luka Garza. This is a big upgrade, especially since Garza’s remaining minutes will end up being against inferior competition. As a result, I think you are looking at a straightforwardly better roster even without appealing to advanced analytics or making contrarian arguments about Brown.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Celtics’ most-used lineup last year was Queta / Brown / Hauser / White / Pritchard. Next year, it should be Tatum / George / White / Pritchard with either Queta or Robinson, and either version would be uncontroversially better than last year’s. The number two lineup was Walsh instead of Hauser. Again, they’ll be better next year. So without disrespecting Brown or even defending the trade per se, I think what you’re left with is that next year’s team will be better than last year’s team was, and last year’s team was good. They also got additional draft picks and future financial flexibility, so the future looks bright to me. But again, I can just do these takes for fun because it’s not my job — I’ve just been a little surprised to see so much focus on the analytics disputes rather than on the basic reality that getting Tatum back from injury and adding Robinson are big upgrades. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-051?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=293205461" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Pragmatic Progressive:</a><span> </span><span>In Ezra Klein’s recent interview with Bill McKibben, they asserted that California has built the equivalent of 13 nuclear power plants in just the last 3 years, in the form of solar and batteries, and questioned why this hasn’t been a bigger story. Assuming the underlying facts are true, does that kind of progress in renewables alter your priors around nuclear energy at all? I know you’re a big proponent based on safety records, probabilities, and trade-offs, but the long tail risk seems pretty large — and more pragmatically, the capital investment seems pretty steep — if we’re truly in a world where scaled renewables are within reach in this generation.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For starters, I personally feel like I’ve read way more excited coverage about battery progress than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d36889b2-fc3e-494b-b84c-e7459c79ff37?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>excited coverage of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s revised Part 53 rule</span></a><span>. So I just don’t think the factual claim is true. I also don’t really think it’s right to say that California’s batteries are “equivalent” to 13 nuclear power plants. Nothing in life provides genuine 24 / 7 / 365 energy that is on all the time, but a 1,100-megawatt nuclear power plant comes a lot closer to that goal than 1,100 megawatts’ worth of batteries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>More broadly, though, I really want to reject the framing that I am a proponent of nuclear power while McKibben is a proponent of solar. It’s not a good idea to get too invested in energy technology fandoms, and it’s not possible to reliably forecast the future course of technological progress. What I am a proponent of is changing the regulatory framework for nuclear power to provide a more balanced assessment of the costs and benefits. I am </span><em><span>also</span></em><span> a proponent of changing the regulatory framework for solar power to make it cheaper and easier to build utility-scale solar projects. A point that I am always trying to make is that while mainstream environmental groups are definitely less hostile to utility-scale solar than they are to nuclear or fossil fuels, they are not actually in favor of the regulatory changes that would make utility-scale solar easier to build either.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-051?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=293174292" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Peter Borsada:</span></a><span> Listening to Ezra Klein’s interview with Bill McKibben and it struck me that you are very quick to attribute institutional opposition to fossil fuels to “the groups” while characterising pro-drilling sentiment as grassroots voter concern (in Texas, Alaska etc.)</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>McKibben obviously takes a radically different view of this and ascribes a lot of agency in energy politics to fossil fuel industry money and lobbying. In the interview, he seems to take the view that, bar that moneyed influence, a more climate focussed electorate would have emerged and steered policy in a greener direction in the decades since Carter first put solar panels on the White House.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Do you underrate the astroturfed element of anti-renewables politics? Does it ultimately not matter if the oil money is chasing after authentic voter sentiment?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the point I ended with above, they are adding solar power more quickly in Texas than they are in California. Is that because the fossil fuel industry has more political clout in Sacramento? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was more than 16 years ago that my friend Julian Sanchez coined the term “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/61b4c096-98ef-405f-ba96-1427223cb4d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>epistemic closure</span></a><span>” to describe the tendency of a political movement to seal itself off from outside information, a phenomenon he saw at the time on the American right. I think that while all of the trends he identified have gotten worse since then, the left-right gap has also narrowed because you see more and more epistemic closure on the left. The view that all resistance to the policy agenda of green NGOs is driven by fossil fuel propaganda creates this kind of loop where the fact that someone is pushing back shows they are a “shill.” So really obvious counterexamples to the fossil-fuel-propaganda theory of everything don’t get raised or heard, and there’s no actual discussion inside the movement about what the strategic or tactical Pew</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Donald Trump surprised me last night. I expected to hear lurid lies about the 2020 election. What he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27b93892-5882-45f9-ab51-e0a48ab3466b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">offered instead</a><span> was mostly dreary innuendo that convinced nobody.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Which is not to say that his speech was free of lies. Indeed, more or less every word he spoke was a lie, including “a,” “and,” and “the.” But the most spectacular lies weren’t about U.S. elections. They were at the beginning, when Trump boasted about America’s place in the world.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here’s the part that caught my eye:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We had transgender for everybody, men in women’s sports, crime ravaging our cities, and the whole world was laughing at us as a nation, but not anymore. Two years ago, our country was dead. Now, we are the hottest country anywhere in the world. </span><strong><span>America is respected like we have never been respected before.</span></strong></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In reality, one of the most spectacular consequences of Trump’s return to power and the mess he has made since has been a collapse of global respect for America. The chart at the top of this post is from Pew’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca83487a-7595-462c-b971-244d12b2ab9b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Global Attitudes Survey</a><span>, but you don’t need a formal survey to know that the world increasingly despises the U.S. Just travel overseas and talk to people.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And it’s not just public opinion. Governments around the world, very much including nations that used to be our most loyal allies, are scrambling to reduce their dependence, economic and military, on an America that can’t be trusted and has also proved itself far weaker than anyone imagined.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why do global attitudes toward the U.S. matter? For one thing, they obviously matter enormously to Trump. Claims that America was a laughingstock under Biden but that everyone now admires him are near the top of many of his speeches. Trump is not, to say the least, a man with great inner strength. He lives for external validation, or the appearance of external validation. Clearly, the delusion that the world is in awe of his prowess is key to his fragile sense of self-worth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">More important, Trump’s boasts about America’s international reputation are part of the case he is building for disrupting and/or rejecting the results of the midterm elections. Trump isn’t just insisting that everything is rigged against him. He’s also insisting that since he’s doing such an incredible job — presidenting like nobody has ever presidented before — nobody should get in his way or place any limits on his power.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s safe to say that at this point nobody who wasn’t already completely in the Trump tank is being persuaded by all this strutting, or indeed by anything Trump said in last night’s low-energy, </span><em>boring</em><span> rant. But remember: At this point, none of what Trump says is really about persuasion. It’s all about laying the groundwork for his attempt to destroy democracy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/dae3500c-f1a1-4987-b0f9-6fd4c8d1d7ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/s3Itb17PXvw" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. 26px;font-size: 16px;">My basic concern is that the U.S. has entered a political era in which reasoned assessment of the evidence, concern for the common good, and deliberation among intellectuals has relatively little effect on policy. When populism, tribalism, and social media shouting rule the nation’s politics, who’s even listening to someone like me?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, I think it’s not that bad. Consider the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7257c0f8-6b7a-4252-adab-d4a37dc2ea2c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">21st Century ROAD to Housing Act</a><span>, which just became law after passing the House and Senate with overwhelming bipartisan majorities, despite Trump’s refusal to sign it. The main provisions of the new law read like a YIMBY’s dream:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Expedited and simplified environmental review for housing projects</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">More federal money for places that build more housing, less money for places that build less</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Some deregulation of prefab home construction and housing finance</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Given the very limited powers that the U.S. federal government has over housing in this country, this is a huge win. These are policies I’ve been advocating for years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Notably, the bill also contains one unhelpful “slopulist” provision: restrictions on the ability of corporate landlords to buy single-family homes. This measure was based on the myth that corporate investors, especially private equity firms, are responsible for the American housing crisis. Would-be populists across the political spectrum, from Elizabeth Warren to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5fce3101-b38a-426a-a910-60d7a997390b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Donald Trump,</a><span> profess to believe in this myth, but it’s just not true — corporate landlords are only </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bd27a94c-1667-4266-b9e1-4dfc869abc48?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a tiny sliver of the housing market</a><span>, and there’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cf1101e-5c88-4d3b-9de8-22d2f94a6e16?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">some evidence that they actually </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cf1101e-5c88-4d3b-9de8-22d2f94a6e16?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">reduce</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cf1101e-5c88-4d3b-9de8-22d2f94a6e16?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> rents</a><span>, especially for low-income tenants. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But because corporate landlords are such a small part of the market, restrictions on their activity are unlikely to have any measurable effect on housing prices nationwide. And the final bill included so many carve-outs — for example, corporations that build housing in order to rent it out are excluded from the restrictions — that its negative impact will probably be very muted. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, we just saw Congress — that dysfunctional institution that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3eae11bd-6314-4149-8900-092e7dddb918?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">everyone hates</a><span> — take action on an important issue in a very reasonable and bipartisan way. It’s a validation of Matt Yglesias’ “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a4493ed-f495-41aa-8729-89552dc8c56b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Secret Congress</a><span>” theory — the idea that our legislators mostly just want to do what’s good for the country, but are prevented from doing so by the partisan anger of their electorates. According to this theory, the way to get good laws passed is to have them remain low-profile, so they don’t arouse the nation’s compulsion to turn everything into a zero-sum politicized food fight. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In other words, there’s still some scope for reasonable individuals and intelligent discourse to make an impact on American policy. But this scope is very limited, because “Secret Congress” has to remain secret — dedicated public servants can tinker around the edges, but can’t enact the kind of bold, sweeping policy program that FDR and Reagan (and to a lesser degree, Obama) were able to carry out. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem is not a lack of good ideas, or a lack of tools for evaluating those ideas. The problem is America’s political economy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Roughly speaking, we have three major political movements — the MAGA right, the socialist left, and the “woke” left. But none of these seems especially interested in the kind of smart, reasonable policies that would significantly improve the material well-being of regular Americans. Their economic programs are all pretty bad. And even if they could be persuaded to support smarter policies, the conflict between the movements will preoccupy them, keeping them focused on culture-war issues. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m not really a political blogger, but an understanding of my country’s political economy seems essential if I want to be a useful intellectual. So I thought I’d give a brief rundown of how I think about the U.S. political situation, and why I think the outlook for a big, constructive policy push is so bleak. I’ll start with a historical analogy. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The Spanish Civil War analogy</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back in 2016, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/826f8170-06fe-4f01-b08b-d5732f48f5a6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">I read a bunch of books on the Spanish Civil War</a><span> of 1936-1939. I immediately saw strong similarities between that conflict and America’s worsening political troubles. In the years since, as America suffered nationwide riots, a coup attempt, military purges, accusations of election theft, and increasingly authoritarian politics, I’ve </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bc480fe6-c64b-40f7-b8ec-12e925eac6c8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">continued to invoke the analogy</a><span>, and I’ve been surprised at how helpful it’s been. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear, </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d900eb3e-abc1-4028-8006-c8e0e03c4002?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">I don’t think</a><span> the U.S. is going to have an actual civil war</span></em><span>. The military would have to fragment and fight itself, as it did in Spain, and I think </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/245f2444-fdec-4f9d-adae-264e9711e815?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">this is unlikely</a><span>. But Americans regularly use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/40dd29e3-ca46-448e-bfbf-760a36136e46?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the language of civil war</a><span> (or “cold civil war”) to define their current political conflicts, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9059ff20-8dc5-4f2e-8b2d-23df49ceae46?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fear of</a><span> an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d012e48-8b10-417d-9977-31ec9c752741?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">actual civil war</a><span> is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c75d6fa-201f-4efe-a0f4-aff98e92509f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">widespread</a><span>. The analogy doesn’t have to be perfect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s a </span><em>very </em><span>brief two-paragraph synopsis of the Spanish Civil War. Basically, Spain in the 1930s was riven by deep, long-standing, intractable class conflict (which also sometimes manifested as </span><em>religious</em><span> conflict between socialists and the Catholic Church). After the country became a democracy in 1931, it see-sawed between left-wing and right-wing governments, with major street clashes between rightists and leftists. In 1934, a bunch of leftist miners </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e402f8c3-a10f-42ec-970a-e6e2f2db9218?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">staged a giant strike</a><span> to protest the admission of some rightists to the government, took over a province of Spain, then tried to turn the strike into a revolution. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The army crushed the revolt, but it led a bunch of right-wing types to panic that if they ever lost another election, there would be a leftist revolution. So in 1936, when a center-left coalition won an election, rightists tried to stage a coup and overthrow the republic. They failed at first, but they captured part of the country. Over the next three years, having already won more of the population and (crucially) the military to their side, they slowly ground down and conquered what remained of the republic. Although both sides were composed of various ideological factions, the rightist (“nationalist”) factions all united around the authority figure of Francisco Franco, while the leftist factions fought each other behind the lines. Both sides committed substantial atrocities, though the nationalists generally committed more. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you want to read more about the war, I suggest:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Antony Beevor’s </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc22c304-a62e-4013-9099-eb4559b68d98?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Battle for Spain</a></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Paul Preston’s </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2af69f3-2cb1-4978-b056-b3d5b5de7542?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Spanish Civil War</a></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>George Orwell’s </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e3efe783-0398-49b1-93f6-4e103d9c251b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Homage to Catalonia</a></em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So how do I see the Spanish Civil War as analogous to America’s current political troubles? Basically:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">A long-standing, intractable social conflict flared into a brief moment of mass revolutionary fervor</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">That almost-revolution panicked various factions of the right, scaring them into uniting behind a radical, authoritarian program</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The most revolutionary factions of the left (the anarchists) were eventually muscled out and dominated by the most disciplined faction (the communists), who then proceeded to lose the war</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The rightists had no idea how to govern the country after their victory, embracing policies that kept Spain poor for decades</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The most important analogy is that although the Spanish Civil War featured a number of different factions, none of the factions had a workable program for governing the country. Spain was basically screwed no matter who it went with, but people still fought very hard for one faction or another, out of a combination of fear, ideology, and opportunism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So let me explain how I think this analogy fits America’s current situation, and why it makes me so pessimistic about governing the country. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The long shadow of 1934 and the long shadow of 2020</h4><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Asturias Revolution of 1934 tends not to be emphasized in discussions of the Spanish Civil War, but it was absolutely crucial. Here is Wikipedia’s description:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The </span><strong>Asturian Revolution</strong><span>…happened in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/01dce934-a705-4e40-9410-dadb0bfc0f67?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Asturias</a><span> from October 4–19, 1934. It started with a mass </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73ba438c-7fa3-4a59-ba77-98c04428f491?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">strike action</a><span> undertaken by miners in Asturias against the new [Spanish] government which included the conservative </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bc496eb8-793f-4ec2-9423-6ebce7aa7d27?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">CEDA</a><span> party.</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;"><span> </span></sup><span>The strike and subsequent demonstrations eventually developed into a violent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88bfbe84-0112-4e4e-9627-66a7e184861c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">revolutionary uprising</a><span> in an attempt to overthrow the government. The revolutionaries took over Asturias by force, killing many of the province's police and religious leaders. Armed with dynamite, rifles, and machine guns, they destroyed religious buildings, such as churches and convents. The rebels officially declared a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fce80dea-3ebd-4876-a71b-53f1fba26983?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Proletarian Revolution</a><span> and instituted a local government in the territory. The rebellion was crushed by the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/66f70fe9-70a7-4c1a-ae5d-1b61e24490fb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Spanish Navy</a><span> and the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53b1b052-3cef-4c73-9823-5322a1da492e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Spanish Republican Army</a><span>, the latter using mainly colonial troops from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6ad9155d-799f-4d9c-a82c-61cf2de8ad1b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Spanish Morocco</a><span>.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This was a </span><em>lot</em><span> more violent than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/983338b9-c368-4ddd-a068-52876ce9c3a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the George Floyd protests</a><span> in the summer of 2020. Although the Floyd protests were a nationwide event involving tens of millions of Americans that did billions of dollars in damage, only </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/05673706-25c4-4d00-8da2-e92e0c4ed0f0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">about 25 people died</a><span> (and several of those were victims of random crime). And yet it </span><em>felt </em><span>like a revolution. In some cities — most famously Seattle — law and order totally broke down in city centers, with local government temporarily </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5d735224-c651-4764-97bd-8013d82ca2fe?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ceding authority to protesters</a><span>. Rioters in D.C. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bea5df7d-6a74-47b2-97dc-a97abec004d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">set fires near the White House</a><span> and the National Mall. </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: were not crushed by the army (though Trump wanted to do that). Instead, they mostly </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f62a3476-57b4-4ebe-ad81-bfc212f97255?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">died down after a month</a><span> and then trickled away over the following year. But in the wake of that nationwide upheaval came sudden and dramatic social changes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Black Lives Matter policy program, which had been formed during the previous six years of smaller-scale protests, was widely implemented by governments, corporations, universities, and nonprofits. DEI programs — many of them explicitly racially discriminatory — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a8d51d2e-4a69-4515-b5e4-bcee5f4276eb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">became commonplace</a><span> across the country. On social media, which by then had come to utterly dominate American social life, “woke” ideology became increasingly intolerant and increasingly dominant. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It wasn’t a military takeover, but in many ways </span><em>this felt like a real revolution</em><span>. It changed how people lived their daily lives and how they thought about themselves and their country. It was the culmination of a cultural wave that had been building for years, but the 2020 protests made it feel as if that cultural wave was backed by force — by the willingness of tens of millions of Americans to pour into the street in service of “woke” ideology. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Americans don’t talk about 2020 much, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b9d278d1-20f4-4002-8762-58470f9e9b6e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">they remember</a><span>. The cultural wave that had been building throughout the 2010s crested in 2020-21, broke, and then receded; by 2023, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3621f144-3976-463b-88b4-75e8d2185bfa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">scholars were marveling</a><span> at how fast “wokeness” was receding from American language and life. But the fear of mass nationwide protests remained. The fear of being “canceled” for not toeing the ideological line of the 2020 protests — and the anger at the memory of such “cancellations” — remained. The people who poured into the street in 2020, or joined cancel-mobs on Twitter in the 2010s, mostly moved on. But the people who felt threatened or canceled did </span><em>not</em><span> move on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Just like the almost-revolution of 1934 panicked the Spanish right, the almost-revolution of 2020 panicked the American right. They became convinced that they were on the brink of a catastrophic, permanent defeat by ruthless ideological enemies bent on destroying them, their property, their culture, and everything they had ever loved. In political terms, to borrow </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c3b0587-6b97-476c-a52d-10461d8b96ba?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a phrase from Sally Paine</a><span>, they felt that they were “on death ground”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It was this desperate fear that drove Republicans of all stripes to unite around Donald Trump, the most corrupt leader in the country’s history. It was this desperate fear that drove them to ally with heterodox leftist figures like Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Tulsi Gabbard — and drove many of them to embrace previously leftist causes like antivax and “anti-imperialism”. It was this fear that drove them to abandon Reaganite conservatism in favor of populism, protectionism, and anything else that looked like it would draw disengaged swing voters into the fold. It was this fear that drove some Republicans to become more sympathetic to Russia. Anything and everything that looked like a possible ally against the all-consuming terror of 2020 was acceptable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is similar to what the Spanish right did in the 1930s. They coalesced behind any leader who seemed strong and ruthless enough to defeat their enemies — first José Sanjurjo, and then Francisco Franco. And they put aside their ideological differences; their coalition included Nazi-like fascists, royalist dead-enders, militant Catholics, militarists, and regular conservatives who just wanted to see order and tradition restored. Unlike the left, this ideological menagerie never fractured; fear was what held it together. (After the war, when this fear had receded, Franco purged many of the most extreme ideologues who had supported him.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For America’s left, meanwhile, the almost-revolution of 2020 proved to be a draining and disheartening event. Almost as soon as the fires went out, most Democrats realized that they had gone too far. The crime wave of 2020-21 began to hollow out the cores of the blue cities that had been the jewels of progressive culture in previous decades.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Anti-police sentiment </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/89b3275a-59e2-42a9-834c-9e8c45988436?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">rapidly waned</a><span>. The DEI regime clearly wasn’t accomplishing its intended purpose of racial justice; instead, it was just pissing a lot of people off. Radical  thinkers like Ibram Kendi, who had been showered with adulation in 2020, were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/500b4b7f-ee70-4044-9ff9-c410a961b154?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">quietly forgotten</a><span> and defunded. “Woke” language </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6b8f09bf-3ad2-4f96-a96e-1e9c0cc1b15d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">began disappearing</a><span> from speech and writing. Popular figures who had been “canceled” during the 2010s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d69b3185-90c9-425a-82bb-393915b04f6e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">made comebacks</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Revolutionary moments almost always peter out like this. In </span><em>Homage to Catalonia</em><span>, Orwell describes how the anarchists of Barcelona had already begun to abandon their radical social experiments — forced changes in language, dress, and social relations — well before the communists and the nationalists came in and crushed them. The ecstasy of a revolution is inherently transient. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To sum up, American politics is now split between a left that would rather forget 2020, and a right that can never let it go. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro
